title: Combining Log Data and Collaborative Dialogue Features to Predict Project Quality in Middle School AI Education
venue: CSEDM’25: 9th Educational Data Mining in Computer Science Education (CSEDM) Workshop
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how to predict the quality of students’ project work during collaborative, project-based AI education. The core problem is that open-ended project-based learning makes it difficult for teachers and researchers to monitor progress and assess emerging project quality before the final product is completed. The authors ask whether two naturally occurring data sources—students’ collaborative dialogue and their interaction logs in a chatbot-building system—can predict process-level indicators of project quality, and whether combining those modalities improves prediction.

The approach centers on multimodal learning analytics rather than testing an instructional treatment against a control group. Students worked in pairs to build science-topic chatbots in the AMBY environment, which logged their actions while audio/video recordings captured their collaboration. The authors synchronized dialogue transcripts with system logs and used features from both sources to predict three outcomes at the intent-submission level: training phrase count (productivity), lexical density (content richness), and lexical variation (diversity of wording). Feedforward neural network regression models were trained and evaluated using log-only, dialogue-only, and combined feature sets.

The study was conducted in spring 2024 in one public middle school science class in the southeastern United States. The broader study included 128 students, with 100 consenting and 94 middle school students (47 pairs) contributing the collaborative sessions analyzed here. Students completed a 10-hour AI literacy module aligned with K-12 AI learning goals, then collaborated across three 40-minute class sessions to develop chatbots on science topics such as climate and living organisms.

The main conclusion is that the usefulness of data modality depends on the outcome being predicted. Log data predicted training phrase count best, dialogue data predicted lexical density best, and both modalities were only modest for lexical variation. Early multimodal fusion improved prediction for training phrase count and slightly for lexical variation, but not for lexical density. The authors conclude that behavioral logs and collaborative dialogue provide complementary but outcome-specific signals about student learning processes in open-ended AI education, and that such models may eventually support teacher analytics or adaptive scaffolding, though the current models are not yet deployment-ready.

identified_tools.name: AMBY
identified_tools.description: A graphical development environment for middle school students to create and test conversational agents/chatbots, define intents, add training phrases and responses, and retrain the chatbot’s intent classification model.
identified_tools.use_case: Students worked in pairs in a 10-hour middle school AI literacy module to build science-topic chatbots in AMBY. The study used AMBY interaction logs plus collaborative dialogue transcripts to predict project-quality proxies during chatbot development.

findings.finding_summary: For predicting training phrase count, log-only features from AMBY outperformed dialogue-only features on the holdout set (AUC = 0.8053, 95% CI [0.7470, 0.8604] vs. 0.5971, 95% CI [0.5250, 0.6671]). Early multimodal fusion further improved prediction to AUC = 0.8301, 95% CI [0.7732, 0.8822]. An ablation removing phrase-add/delete and add-response dependent features reduced AUCs to 0.6865 (log only) and 0.6759 (combined).
findings.measure: Holdout AUC for predicting training phrase count (productivity/completeness proxy) from AMBY logs, dialogue, and combined features

findings.finding_summary: For predicting lexical density of chatbot training phrases, dialogue-only features performed better than AMBY log-only features on the holdout set (AUC = 0.6551, 95% CI [0.5920, 0.7168] vs. 0.5112, 95% CI [0.4556, 0.5655]). The combined model underperformed the dialogue-only model, with AUC = 0.5700, 95% CI [0.5042, 0.6352].
findings.measure: Holdout AUC for predicting lexical density of training phrases (content richness proxy)

findings.finding_summary: For predicting lexical variation of chatbot training phrases, both AMBY log-only and dialogue-only models performed modestly on the holdout set (AUC = 0.6016, 95% CI [0.5418, 0.6615] and 0.5260, 95% CI [0.4579, 0.5933], respectively). Multimodal fusion yielded only a slight improvement to AUC = 0.6089, 95% CI [0.5438, 0.6727], which the authors note is likely not significant based on overlapping confidence intervals.
findings.measure: Holdout AUC for predicting lexical variation of training phrases (word diversity proxy)

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical primary study with 94 middle school students, but it is correlational/predictive learning analytics research rather than an intervention evaluation with randomization or a quasi-experimental comparison on student outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports predictive performance (AUCs) for project-quality proxies rather than causal treatment effects on learning outcomes. Results are modest to mixed and do not establish clear educational impact magnitude.
